extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) counsel, and respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A formal USPTO/OED initial decision setting out findings of fact, statutory/regulatory violations (37 C.F.R. provisions), and the sanctioning framework for attorney misconduct (defaults, failures to respond, client neglect, dishonesty, and cooperation with investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to answer complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not timely answer the complaint, the allegations are deemed admitted and may be adopted as the court's findings of fact; default judgment may follow (illustrated by Respondent being deemed to have admitted the Complaint's allegations).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — Disreputable or gross misconduct: failure to perform retained services
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct by failing to perform services that he was retained to perform on behalf of a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the decision: allowing a patent or trademark application to become abandoned without client knowledge or consent; failing to take steps to revive an application; failing to protect client's IP rights; failing to inform clients about the status of their matters. The Court found these facts sufficient to violate § 10.23(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a) & (b) via 10.23(c)(2)(i) — Knowingly giving false or misleading information
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes knowingly giving false or misleading information or knowingly participating in giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with any immediate, prospective or pending business before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where practitioner knowingly misinformed clients about the status of their applications (e.g., telling a client an application was "on track" when deadlines had been missed). The decision treats knowingly misleading statements to clients about Office matters as a violation under these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a) & (b) via 10.23(c)(8) — Failing to notify client of Office correspondence when reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to inform a client of correspondence received from the Office when the correspondence could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client, and is correspondence which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances that the client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies this standard where the practitioner received Notices of Allowance, Notices to File Corrected Application Papers, Office Actions, and Notices of Abandonment but did not timely notify clients. Failure to notify in such circumstances is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — Neglect of legal matter entrusted to practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where practitioner allowed client matters (patent or trademark applications) to become abandoned without taking steps to remedy or protect the client's interests. The decision finds neglect where the practitioner did not act after receiving Office notices and permitted abandonment without client consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Failing to provide competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to provide competent representation to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds § 11.101 violated where, on or after May 3, 2013, the practitioner failed to take steps to revive abandoned applications, failed to transfer matters as promised, and otherwise failed to protect clients' IP interests. Competence includes following through on agreed services and necessary actions after Office notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where the practitioner repeatedly failed to respond to Office Actions, Notices, or clients' inquiries, resulting in abandonment of applications. The decision treats lack of timely response to required Office deadlines and client follow-ups as failure of diligence/promptness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) & (3) — Failing to keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where the practitioner did not inform clients of Office Actions, Notices of Allowance/Abandonment, or other significant correspondence, and did not reasonably consult with clients about legal consequences or options. Failure to inform or consult is a violation under these subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds § 11.804(c) violated where the practitioner provided false or misleading information to clients about the status of their matters (e.g., lying that matters were progressing when deadlines had been missed), which constitutes dishonesty and supports disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with OED disciplinary investigations / respond to RFIs and requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to respond substantively to OED Requests for Information and follow-up inquiries; failure to respond or to provide supporting documentation can be deemed non-cooperation and aggravating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case, OED sent RFIs requesting explanations for abandoned applications and supporting documentation; the respondent's failure to answer the RFIs and a Lack of Response letter was used as evidence of obstruction and aggravation. Prior failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigations was also noted as an aggravating factor (e.g., prior North Carolina matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these factors: duty violations (fiduciary duties, competence, diligence, communication), respondent's state of mind (found knowing/intentional), actual/potential injury (financial loss, loss of IP rights), and aggravating factors (prior disciplinary offense, acceptance of prepaid fees not fulfilled, dishonest/selfish motive, multiple offenses/pattern of misconduct across many applications, obstruction of the disciplinary process). These factors guide severity of sanction (here, exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-sanction responsibilities (37 C.F.R. § 11.58 reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directs excluded/suspended practitioners to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 regarding responsibilities in cases of suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notifies the respondent of obligations upon exclusion (refers to § 11.58). While the decision does not reproduce § 11.58 text, practitioners are required to follow those regulatory duties after suspension/exclusion (e.g., client notifications, file transfer/retention obligations).
